warmup.q: A transfer goes over TLS on TCP to an API server, through an idempotent Kafka producer with exactly-once processing, into a serializable PostgreSQL transaction. The phone's request times out after the server has committed, and the phone sends it again. How many transfers does the ledger record?
options: One, because every layer on the path is exactly-once
Two, because no layer on the path can tell the retry from a new transfer
One, because TCP's sequence numbers drop the repeated request
None, because the timeout rolls back the first transaction
warmup.why: Each guarantee holds inside its own layer and says nothing about the retry. The retry is a new TCP connection with fresh sequence numbers, a new send() with a new producer sequence number, and a new, perfectly valid transaction. Only something that knows the two requests are one user intent can drop the second, and that knowledge starts on the phone. The first option is the trap: stacking exactly-once layers feels like it should add up to exactly-once overall. The last option fails because the server's commit doesn't know the phone stopped waiting.

sections.h: A retried transfer moves the money twice
sections.html:
A customer on a train sends 45.00 from the banking app. The server commits the transfer 80 ms later. The response is lost in a tunnel. After 10 seconds the app gives up waiting and sends the request again, on a new connection. The server sees a well-formed transfer request and commits it. The account is 90.00 lighter.

Which part was wrong? None of them, taken alone. TCP delivered each request exactly once on its connection. The database ran each transaction atomically and committed each one once. The app did what a client must: when it hears nothing back, it can't tell whether the request was lost or only the response (the Faults, time and truth track's lesson on partial failure). Retrying is the only way to make sure the transfer happens at all.

The duplicate exists only at a level none of those parts can see: the customer meant one transfer, and two arrived. The database can't know it. To the database, two identical transfers a few seconds apart are as plausible as a retry, because people do pay the same amount twice. Two-phase commit (the Transactions track) can't help either. It lets a coordinator find out whether an in-doubt transaction committed, but the phone is not a participant in it, and the hop from the phone to the server is exactly where the doubt began. Redirecting the browser after a successful POST doesn't help when the POST's response is the thing that was lost.

So the information that would let you suppress the duplicate exists only on the phone, at the moment the user taps send. The fix this lesson builds is to give that tap an identity and carry it to the place where money moves. First, the principle behind it, and why every layer below the application has the same blind spot.

The Try it plays the train ride twice. Without an id that survives the retry, two attempts make two ledger rows and 90.00 leaves the account. With one id per tap and a unique constraint on the ledger, the same two attempts make one row.

try.title: Lose one response
steps: Run the demo from the labs folder. It sends one 45.00 transfer whose first response is lost, so the phone retries once. It runs twice: with a new request id on every attempt, then with one id per tap and a unique check at the ledger.
Predict for each run: how many records reach the broker, and how many rows reach the ledger?
In the second run the broker still has two records. Why is that fine?

code.title: RetryDemo.kt (excerpt)
code.html: val lostFirst = Endpoint { r, intent, attempt -> server.call(r, intent, attempt) // the server does the work... attempt > 1 // ...and the first response is lost } for (attempt in 1..3) { val id = if (oneIdPerTap || attempt == 1) firstId else "req-%06d".format(++ids) if (lostFirst.call(Request(id, "acc-01", "acc-02", 4_500), 0, attempt)) break }

try.expect:
a new request id per attempt, no unique check:
  attempts sent: 2, ids req-000001, req-000002
  records in the broker: 2
  ledger row: req-000001 acc-01 -> acc-02 45.00
  ledger row: req-000002 acc-01 -> acc-02 45.00
  acc-01 1000.00 -> 910.00, moved 90.00
one request id per tap, UNIQUE (request_id) in the ledger:
  attempts sent: 2, ids req-000001, req-000001
  records in the broker: 2
  ledger row: req-000001 acc-01 -> acc-02 45.00
  acc-01 1000.00 -> 955.00, moved 45.00

Both runs put two records in the broker, because the server really did receive two requests. The second run is correct anyway: the duplicate is dropped at the last step, where the money moves, and nothing before that step had to be perfect.

sections.h: The end-to-end argument: only the endpoints know what correct means
sections.html:
In 1984 Jerome Saltzer, David Reed and David Clark of MIT published "End-to-End Arguments in System Design" (ACM Transactions on Computer Systems 2(4)). Its question was where in a layered system a function belongs, and their worked case was moving a file from the disk of computer A to the disk of computer B without damage.

They listed what can go wrong. The disk at A can return bad data. The file system, the transfer program or the network code can make a mistake while buffering and copying, at either end. The processor or memory can have a transient error during a copy. The network can drop, corrupt, lose or duplicate packets. And either host can crash partway through. Now suppose the network guarantees reliable delivery, with checksums, sequence numbers and retries inside it. It fixes the network threat and none of the others. A bug that corrupts a buffer on host B happens after the network has done its job perfectly.

The only complete check sits at the ends. Host B reads the file back from its own disk, computes a checksum, and A compares it with the original's; if they differ, start again. That check is needed anyway, so a reliable network isn't required for correctness. It only makes retries rarer, which is a performance gain. The paper's principle is that such a function can be implemented completely "only with the knowledge and help of the application" at the endpoints, and a partial version lower down is justified only as a performance enhancement.

The paper applies the same reasoning to duplicate suppression, and its example could be today's. A network that suppresses its own duplicates still can't suppress the duplicates the application creates through its own retries: a user who gets no answer and tries again produces a message that, to the network, is simply a new one. Only the application can recognise its own repeats.

The same argument covers two more functions you rely on. One is integrity. TCP's 16-bit checksum and TLS's authentication tag protect bytes while they cross one connection. A bug in your service that corrupts an amount, or a flipped bit on a disk, happens outside any connection and passes every check. Lesson 5 of this track builds end-to-end checks for stored data. The other is confidentiality. TLS encrypts each hop, and a load balancer that terminates TLS reads plaintext. Encryption that must survive every intermediary needs keys only the endpoints hold.

None of this says the lower layers are useless. TCP's retransmission saves you from retrying a whole transfer after every lost packet. The lower layers make the common case fast. Correctness still has to be checked at the endpoints.

try.title: What each mechanism covers, and where it stops
steps: For each mechanism, write what it protects and the first thing on the phone-to-ledger path that it can't see.

1. TCP sequence numbers. 2. TLS between the phone and the load balancer. 3. Kafka's idempotent producer. 4. Kafka exactly-once (transactions plus read_committed). 5. A PostgreSQL transaction at SERIALIZABLE. 6. Temporal retrying an activity that calls the card issuer. 7. An Idempotency-Key sent to the card issuer. 8. A request id made on the phone and kept UNIQUE in the ledger.
try.expect:
1. Repeated and reordered bytes within one connection. Can't see: a retry on a new connection.
  2. Eavesdropping and tampering between the phone and the load balancer. Can't see: anything after TLS ends, in plaintext inside your network.
  3. A producer's own resend of a batch after a lost ack. Can't see: a second send() of the same transfer, which gets a new sequence number.
  4. Reading, processing and writing within Kafka, with the offset commit in the same transaction. Can't see: a write to PostgreSQL or a call to the issuer inside the loop.
  5. Concurrent transactions interfering with each other. Can't see: two transactions that are both valid, one being a retry of the other.
  6. A crashed or failed activity being run again. Can't see: whether the issuer already captured the payment the first time; it makes duplicates more likely, not less.
  7. Duplicate captures at the issuer, for retries that send the same key. Can't see: your own ledger.
  8. The whole path: every retry of one tap, at any hop, is recognised at the final write. Its limit is time: a retry after the id is pruned is new again (section 5).

refs.title: Saltzer, Reed and Clark, End-to-End Arguments in System Design (ACM TOCS, 1984)

sections.h: Every layer's exactly-once stops at its own edge
sections.html:
Here is the path a transfer takes in this lesson's lab, and the four faults the lab injects, one at each hop.

The phone sends the request over HTTP, on TCP, to the API server. Fault one: the network delivers the request twice on that connection, as a retransmission whose original wasn't lost. Fault two: the server commits, the response is lost, and the phone retries on a new connection. The server produces a record to the broker. Fault three: the broker appends it, its acknowledgement is lost, and the producer resends the batch. A consumer reads the record, inserts a ledger row in PostgreSQL, and commits its offset. Fault four: the consumer dies after the insert and before the commit, so the record is delivered again.

Each layer has its own guard, and each guard is correct within its scope.

  • TCP numbers every byte on a connection and drops bytes it has already delivered. It catches fault one. A retry opens a new connection with fresh numbers, so fault two gets through.
  • The idempotent producer (the Messaging track's lesson on producer idempotence) tags each batch with a producer id and a sequence number, and the broker refuses a pair it has appended. It catches fault three. When the server handles the phone's retry, it calls send() again and gets the next sequence number, so fault two gets through again.
  • Kafka's exactly-once (the Messaging track's lesson on transactions) commits a consumer's offsets and its Kafka outputs together. The ledger row is in PostgreSQL, outside that transaction, so fault four leaves a row behind that Kafka can't take back.
  • The database runs each transaction atomically. The retry from fault two and the redelivery from fault four are each a valid new transaction.

Durable execution engines have the same edge. The Encoding track's lesson on durable execution showed that Temporal records a step's result once, but the step itself runs at least once.

The lab measures it. 1,000 transfers go through the same faults with each guard switched on in turn. With none, the ledger ends up with 103 extra rows, and 53,025.23 moves that nobody asked to move. TCP's sequence numbers bring it to 78, and the idempotent producer to 47. The 47 left are lost responses and consumer crashes, the two faults that happen above every layer: one in the client's retry, one in the gap between two systems. A request id checked at the ledger brings it to 0.

The stepper follows one transfer through all four faults.

try.title: Switch the guards on one at a time
steps: Run the demo. It sends 1,000 transfers through the lab's pipeline four times, with the same faults each time: 2% of requests repeated on their connection, 3% of responses lost, 2% of broker acks lost, 1.5% of consumers crashing between the insert and the offset commit.
Predict which variant removes the most duplicates, and how many are left before the last one.
Run it with another seed, -Pargs=7. Do the counts change? Does the shape?

code.title: DuplicatesDemo.kt
code.html: for (v in Variant.entries) { val r = Pipeline.run(v, seed) println("%-11s %16d %16s".format(v, r.duplicates, "%,.2f".format(r.extraCents / 100.0))) }

try.expect:
variant       duplicate rows      extra money
NONE                     103        53,025.23
TRANSPORT                 78        38,375.76
BROKER                    47        23,215.72
END_TO_END                 0             0.00

Each lower layer removes its own share and no more, and no layer below the application gets to zero, because the remaining faults are retries and redeliveries that look new to everything below the endpoint. Another seed gives different counts with the same shape, and END_TO_END is 0 for every seed; the lab's property test checks that for 40 random seeds.

video.title: A retried transfer, and the id that stops the duplicate

sections.h: One operation id from the phone to a unique constraint
sections.html:
The fix has three parts, and each one is easy to get slightly wrong.

First, make the id where the intent is. The phone creates one id when the user taps send, or when it renders the form, and keeps it for every attempt at that one transfer. A UUIDv7 works well: it's unique without coordination and starts with a timestamp, so new ids land at the right-hand edge of a B-tree index instead of all over it (PostgreSQL 18 can generate one with uuidv7()). The classic bug is making the id inside the retry loop. Every attempt then has its own id, and nothing downstream can match them. The lab's phone ships with that bug.

Second, carry it through every hop. The id travels in the HTTP Idempotency-Key header, the Encoding track's lesson on calling other services gave its rules, and the Caching track's lesson on idempotency keys built the Redis record that answers retries fast. The IETF draft for the header is at revision 08 (October 2026) and isn't an RFC yet. The API server copies the id into a Kafka record header, and the consumer copies it into the ledger row. Any hop that drops it, or makes a fresh one because it seemed tidier, reopens the hole for everything after it.

Third, enforce it at the final write, in the same transaction as the effect. The ledger table has the request id as its primary key. The consumer inserts the row with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING and moves the money only if a row was inserted:

WITH ins AS (
    INSERT INTO derive_ledger (request_id, from_account, to_account, cents)
    VALUES ('019a5e3c-4b7d-7f21-9c3e-2d4a6b8c0e1f', 'acc-01', 'acc-02', 4500)
    ON CONFLICT (request_id) DO NOTHING
    RETURNING from_account, to_account, cents
)
UPDATE derive_accounts a
SET balance_cents = a.balance_cents
    + CASE WHEN a.account_id = ins.to_account THEN ins.cents ELSE -ins.cents END
FROM ins
WHERE a.account_id IN (ins.from_account, ins.to_account);

The first run reports UPDATE 2. Running the identical statement again, the redelivery, reports UPDATE 0, and the balances don't move. It holds under concurrency at PostgreSQL's default, read committed. In the Try it, a second session running the same statement while the first is uncommitted waits on the first one's unique-index entry for 1.5 seconds, then reports UPDATE 0.

Why a constraint, and not a check in code? A SELECT for the id followed by an INSERT is check-then-act. At read committed, two concurrent copies both find nothing and both insert, the phantom problem from the Transactions track's lesson on write skew. Bailis and colleagues' 2015 study of Rails applications, "Feral Concurrency Control", found exactly this: uniqueness validations in application code let duplicates through under concurrent requests. The database checks a unique index at every isolation level.

The ledger table now doubles as a log of every request that moved money. Balances could be derived from it downstream, which is where lesson 1 started.

try.title: Post the same transfer twice, then twice at once
steps: From the labs folder: docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait, then docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz.

Create the tables:

CREATE TABLE derive_accounts (account_id text PRIMARY KEY, balance_cents bigint NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE derive_ledger (
    request_id   uuid PRIMARY KEY,
    from_account text   NOT NULL,
    to_account   text   NOT NULL,
    cents        bigint NOT NULL CHECK (cents > 0),
    created_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
INSERT INTO derive_accounts VALUES ('acc-01', 100000), ('acc-02', 0);
Run the section's statement twice, then SELECT * FROM derive_accounts ORDER BY 1; and SELECT count(*) FROM derive_ledger;. Predict both before you look.

Now concurrency. Open a second psql session. In the first: BEGIN;, then the statement with a new id (change 4b7d to aaaa). Don't commit. In the second, run the same statement with the same new id. Watch it wait. Commit the first, and read the second's result.
Stop with docker compose -f env/postgres.yml down -v.

code.title: what to check after the two runs
code.html: SELECT account_id, balance_cents FROM derive_accounts ORDER BY 1; SELECT count(*) AS ledger_rows FROM derive_ledger; SHOW transaction_isolation;

try.expect:
The two runs, then the checks:

UPDATE 2
UPDATE 0
 account_id | balance_cents
------------+---------------
 acc-01     |         95500
 acc-02     |          4500
 ledger_rows
-------------
           1
 transaction_isolation
-----------------------
 read committed

The concurrent run (here the first session held its transaction open for 2 seconds):

session A: BEGIN
session A: UPDATE 2
session B: (waits on A's uncommitted row in the unique index)
session A: COMMIT
session B: UPDATE 0        -- after waiting 1528 ms

The second insert can't decide whether its id is taken until the first transaction commits or aborts, so it waits, then finds the row and does nothing. Had A rolled back, B's insert would have gone in. Either way exactly one transfer happens, at read committed, without any application lock.

sections.html:
The id isn't free, and each of its costs is a design decision you make once.

The first is memory. The ledger has to remember each id for as long as any client might still retry it, because a retry after the id is forgotten is a new transfer. The Try it replays 100,000 transfers with realistic retry delays: most retries come within seconds, some phones were in the background for an hour, a few were offline for days. A 1-minute window lets 292 duplicates through, 1 hour lets 184, 24 hours 9, and 7 days none. Stripe keeps its idempotency keys for at least 24 hours, and a key reused after it was pruned starts a new request. For money, keep ids longer than the longest retry your clients can make, or make clients stop retrying blindly past that age and ask the server what happened instead.

That memory takes space. At 1,000 transfers a second, a 24-hour window holds 86.4 million ids, about 8.6 GB at an assumed 100 bytes per id with its index entry. When the id is the ledger's own primary key, as in the SQL above, it's never forgotten, and the ledger carries that index forever. A separate request-id table, written in the same transaction and partitioned by day, lets ids expire with a cheap DROP of an old partition instead of a DELETE that bloats the table.

Every transfer also does one more write: a unique-index probe and insert, in the same transaction. That's cheap with UUIDv7, whose inserts go to the right-hand edge of the index (the Storage engines track's lesson on B+trees), and noticeably dearer with random UUIDv4, which touches a random page each time.

The id has to live where the effect lives, because the check must be in the same transaction. If the ledger is sharded by account (the Partitioning track), key the id table by the paying account too, so the check and the money move on one shard.

A client that retries wants the result of its first attempt, and a bare "duplicate" error doesn't say whether the transfer went through. So the server keeps the first response under the id and replays it, which is the record the Caching track's lesson built. It also stores a fingerprint of the request body and rejects the same id with different contents (HTTP 422 in the IETF draft), because that is a client bug, not a retry.

Finally, the guarantee is only as good as the least careful service on the path. Code review has to treat "copies the request id into the outgoing record" the way it treats "validates the amount". Each external call carries the id downstream too: the card issuer's own idempotency key is how a capture survives your retries.

try.title: How long must the ledger remember?
steps: Run the demo. It sends 100,000 transfers, 3% of them sent again later after delays from a few seconds to three days, through a ledger that forgets ids older than its window.
Predict how many duplicates a 1-hour window lets through. More or less than 1 in 1,000?
Find the shortest window with no duplicates in this run, and read its storage cost. Is it worth it for transfers? For "like" buttons?

code.title: WindowDemo.kt (excerpt)
code.html: for ((t, i) in events) { if (t - lastPrune >= minute) { ledger.prune(olderThan = t - window); lastPrune = t } ledger.postOnce(Row("req-$i", "a", "b", 1), now = t) }

try.expect:
100,000 transfers, 2,891 sent again later
window       duplicate rows        id table at 1,000/s
1 minute                292           60,000 ids, 6 MB
1 hour                  184      3,600,000 ids, 360 MB
24 hours                  9     86,400,000 ids, 8.6 GB
7 days                    0   604,800,000 ids, 60.5 GB

An hour still lets 184 in 100,000 through, almost 2 per 1,000, because the phones that were offline retry after the window. Seven days removes them all in this run at 60 GB of ids (the sizes assume 100 bytes per id). For transfers that is cheap insurance. For a "like" button, a duplicate is harmless and a minute is plenty. The window is a business decision with a number attached.

refs.title: IETF draft: The Idempotency-Key HTTP Header Field

analogy: A cheque number. When you write a cheque, its number is printed on it before you hand it over. If the bank receives the same cheque twice, because you posted it and then handed in a photocopy when it seemed lost, the number lets the bank pay it once. The postal service can't do that for you, however reliable it is, because it doesn't know two envelopes hold the same cheque. The analogy breaks at memory: a bank keeps cheque numbers for years at little cost, while your ledger pays for every id it remembers, so you have to choose how long a retry can still be recognised.
world: In a Quarkus payment service, make the request id part of the API contract: the mobile app and partner clients send Idempotency-Key (a UUIDv7 made when the payment is created on the client), a JAX-RS filter rejects POSTs without one, and the resource puts it in the MDC so it shows in every log line. When the service produces to Kafka, copy it into a record header, and have every consumer read it from there instead of making its own. In the consumer that writes Oracle, make it the primary key of the ledger row, insert that row first in the transaction that updates the balance, and treat ORA-00001 (unique constraint violated) as "already done": Oracle rolls back only the failed statement, so you skip the balance update and commit nothing. When a Temporal activity calls the card issuer, derive the issuer's idempotency key from the request id (plus the step name if one request makes several calls), because the activity will run again after a worker crash. And agree the retention with the mobile team: if the app retries queued payments after a night offline, an id table pruned at one hour will double-charge.
mistake: The most common mistake is generating the idempotency key on the server, or inside the client's retry loop: the API gateway assigns a UUID to each incoming request, or the HTTP client library adds a fresh key per attempt. It looks right in logs, since every request has a key, and tests pass, because tests rarely retry after a lost response. But a retry is a new request to the gateway and a new attempt to the library, so it gets a new key, and the ledger sees two different keys for one payment. The key has to be created once per user intent, before the first attempt, by the code that knows what the user meant, and reused for every retry. The second most common mistake is checking the key in a separate store (a Redis lookup, or a SELECT before the INSERT) instead of in the same transaction as the money movement; a crash or a concurrent duplicate gets through the gap.

worked.title: Carry one id from the tap to the ledger

steps.say: Make the id once, outside the retry loop. The phone's intent is the tap, so the id belongs to the tap, not to an attempt.
steps.code: fun send(server: Endpoint, intent: Int, from: String, to: String, cents: Long): List<String> { val id = newId() // one id per tap val sent = ArrayList<String>() for (attempt in 1..maxAttempts) { sent += id // the same id on every attempt if (server.call(Request(id, from, to, cents), intent, attempt)) break } return sent }

steps.say: Know what each lower guard does, so you don't rely on it for more. TCP drops a repeat inside one connection; the idempotent broker drops a resend of the same (producer, sequence). Both are performance aids here.
steps.code: fun receive(seq: Long, request: Request): Request? { if (seq <= highestDelivered) return null // a retransmitted copy highestDelivered = seq return request } // broker: a resend of a batch it already has if (idempotent) appended[producerId to seq]?.let { return it }

steps.say: Check the id and move the money in one step. In the lab, one method; in PostgreSQL, one statement or one transaction.
steps.code: fun postOnce(row: Row, now: Long): Boolean { if (row.requestId in seen) return false // the unique index refuses it seen[row.requestId] = now post(row) // the money moves only here return true }

steps.say: Choose the window from the client's retry horizon. Forgotten ids make retries new again.
steps.code: ledger.prune(olderThan = now - window) // window >= longest client retry // 1 minute: 292 duplicates per 100,000 in the Try it // 1 hour: 184 // 24 hours: 9 // 7 days: 0

lab.title: Count duplicate ledger rows with each layer's guard, then fix it end to end
steps: Run the tests once from the labs folder. All 12 fail.

Read Pipeline.kt and Faults.kt; both are finished. Server opens a new Connection per attempt and produces to the Broker; Consumer writes the Ledger and commits its offset, unless the fault plan crashes it in between. Each fault is decided by a hash of the event's name, so all four variants see the same faults.
In Hops.kt, write Connection.receive and Broker.append. The transport and broker tests in HopsTest pass.
Write Ledger.postOnce: refuse a request id that's already in seen; otherwise record it and post the row, in that one method.

Fix the bug in Phone.send: it makes a new id per attempt. Run all the tests. PipelineTest checks the counts from this lesson: 103, 78 and 47 duplicates for the first three variants and 0 end to end, plus a property test over 40 random seeds.
hints: Connection.receive: keep highestDelivered; return null when seq <= highestDelivered, otherwise store seq and return the request.
Broker.append: when idempotent, appended[producerId to seq]?.let { return it } first. Then append a Record(records.size.toLong(), request, trace) and remember its offset under the pair.
postOnce must not call post when it returns false. If the ledger posts a request id once shows the money moved twice, check the order.
If duplicates fall at each layer shows END_TO_END above 0 while the ledger test passes, the phone is still sending a new id per attempt.

drill.title: The end-to-end write from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write the PostgreSQL statement that records a transfer with request id :rid and moves the money only if the id is new. Then list, in one line each, the guard at each of the four hops and the fault it can't see.

answer.html: WITH ins AS ( INSERT INTO ledger (request_id, from_account, to_account, cents) VALUES (:rid, :from, :to, :cents) ON CONFLICT (request_id) DO NOTHING -- a repeat inserts nothing RETURNING from_account, to_account, cents ) UPDATE accounts a SET balance_cents = a.balance_cents + CASE WHEN a.account_id = ins.to_account THEN ins.cents ELSE -ins.cents END FROM ins -- no row inserted: no money moves WHERE a.account_id IN (ins.from_account, ins.to_account); -- TCP sequence numbers: can't see a retry on a new connection -- idempotent producer: can't see a second send() of the same transfer -- Kafka exactly-once: can't see a write to the database inside the loop -- the database transaction: can't tell a retry from a new transaction

recap: A client that hears nothing must retry, and can't tell a lost request from a lost response, so retries create duplicates that no lower layer can recognise.

The end-to-end argument (Saltzer, Reed and Clark, 1984): a function like duplicate suppression, integrity checking or encryption can be done completely only at the endpoints; lower-layer versions are performance aids.

TCP dedupes within one connection, the idempotent producer within one producer's resends, Kafka exactly-once within Kafka, and a transaction within itself. In the lab they cut 103 duplicates to 78 and then 47, never to 0.
Make one id per user intent on the client, carry it through every hop (HTTP header, record header), and enforce it with a unique constraint in the same transaction as the effect. That gets to 0.
A unique index works at read committed; check-then-insert in code doesn't.

The cost is remembering ids for the whole retry horizon (24 hours of ids at 1,000 a second is about 86 million), an index write per request, ids that live where the effect lives, and every hop carrying the id.

explain.prompt: A colleague says: "We use TLS, Kafka with exactly-once, and Oracle transactions, so we can't double-charge." Explain where that reasoning breaks, and what you'd add.
explain.answer: Each of those is correct inside its own layer and blind to the duplicate that matters. When a phone's request times out after we committed, the phone retries, and the retry is a new TLS session, a new TCP connection, a new Kafka send with a new sequence number and a new, valid Oracle transaction. Kafka's exactly-once covers Kafka writes and offsets, so a consumer that dies after the Oracle insert and before its offset commit writes the row again on redelivery. The only party that knows two requests are one payment is the client that sent them. So the client makes one id per payment before the first attempt and reuses it on every retry, every hop copies it (HTTP header, Kafka header, ledger column), and the ledger keeps it unique, checked in the same transaction that moves the money. The lower layers still matter, because they make retries rarer, but correctness comes from that one check. We also have to keep the ids at least as long as the app can retry, which for offline phones means days.

deeper.html:
Saltzer, Reed and Clark's other examples. The paper also applies the argument to delivery acknowledgements (a network-level ack says a message arrived, not that the application acted on it), to detecting host crashes, and to message ordering. Its cautionary note is useful: the argument isn't a rule that lower layers must be dumb. Where a lower layer can do something cheaply that removes most failures, do it, and still check at the ends.

Payments across shards without atomic commit. If the payer's and the payee's accounts live on different shards, the request id is what lets you skip two-phase commit. Append the request once to the payer's shard. A single-threaded processor there checks funds and emits a debit, a credit and a fee event, all carrying the request id; every processor downstream applies events once per id. After a crash, the processor reruns from its log, makes the same decision and emits the same ids, which downstream ignores. Kleppmann, Beresford and Svingen describe this design in "Online Event Processing" (CACM, 2019), and lesson 4 of this track builds the constraint side of it.

Stripe's v2 API goes further. For API v1, Stripe stores the first response under the key and replays it, including errors. For API v2, a retry with the same key drives failed or partially failed work to completion when it can, instead of replaying an old failure. That's the same end-to-end idea with the server taking on more of the recovery.

Exactly-once is a property of effects. Every system that advertises exactly-once (Kafka, Flink, Temporal, Step Functions) delivers or executes at least once and arranges for the effect to count once, within its boundary. When you cross the boundary, you bring your own id.

The framing of exactly-once effects, the end-to-end argument applied to data systems and the operation-id pattern follows Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 13.
